title: Voice (sustained sung vowels)
reference_instrument: adult male voice, sustained vowels (VocalSet long tones, CC BY 4.0)
summary: Sustained vowels on C3, C4 and F4, with no words. The tract is another man's, from MRI of spoken German vowels, so the tilt follows his vowels, not the singers'. Harmonics-to-noise is inside its ruler on 13 of 14 pages, but the shape is wrong even where the total is right. A vocal fold model self-oscillates against that tract (two-mass on the phrases and 13 of the 14 notes, Story and Titze's three-mass body-cover fold on F4-a), and the sound is read at a simulated microphone 0.30 m from the mouth, 45 degrees off axis. No source waveform or formant filter is applied. One scale on the fold stiffnesses (Q on the body-cover fold) is the one model-only factor: trimmed on the model alone, it puts each card near its written note, so pitch isn't evidence. The graded notes are straight tones with a slow and a fast pitch row, a small cycle-to-cycle shimmer in the glottal pulse, and no vibrato. The phrases carry vibrato in place of the slow row, with the fast row and the shimmer under it, and each vowel there is its own render, joined by crossfades. The /a/ at six pitches and the vowel ladder further down are older renders on earlier tracts.
physics_present: On the phrases and 13 of the 14 notes, two-mass vocal folds on Ishizaka and Flanagan's 1972 law as printed, for the glottal flow and the forces on the masses, as a mirror pair, with masses and base stiffnesses from the licensed model-card pack. The oscillation isn't imposed: it comes from the fold, the flow, collision and the tract loop.

Story and Titze's three-mass body-cover fold (NCVS Status and Progress Report 6, 1994), case C of their Table 1, with that report's own pressure and flow law, on F4-a only. Q, one scale on its four stiffnesses, is the one model-only factor: trimmed to within 3 cents of the written note, it ends at 4.109 against a start of 4.633. Story and Titze's 0.8 kPa lung pressure isn't applied; the breath stays the card's player row. The fold misses its own paper's Table 2 on our test tube, and the paper's tube isn't printed. The other twelve pages it was tried on keep the two-mass fold: on the five C3 pages the measured tract holds its pitch off the note; on C4-a, C4-o, C4-u and F4-o its pitch jumps across the note between nearly equal values of Q; and C4-e, C4-i and F4-e reached their notes but didn't pass the posting rule. On the measured C3 tracts this fold's pitch stays at 125–157 Hz whatever its stiffness (Q 0.45–1.29); on a plain 17.5 cm tube the same fold at the same breath sings 108–114 Hz. The tract holds its pitch, so there are no C3 pages.

A measured tract on every page: subject 1 of the Dresden Vocal Tract Dataset (Birkholz et al. 2020, CC0), a man in MRI of spoken German vowels, tense or lax by a rule fixed before any grade. The cut from his 3-D model to one dimension is ours (91 to 113 sections), and the dataset's own printed area functions aren't used.
Viscothermal loss and a flanged-piston mouth load from the transfer-matrix duct.
The cited yielding wall (the Flanagan setting as given by Birkholz, Haesner and Kuerbis 2022) on all 14 cards, including C4-u-rigid, whose name comes from an older comparison.
Sound at the microphone: mouth flow radiated through a baffled circular opening, 0.30 m away at 45 degrees off axis. The pressure inside the tract is never the output.

Slow pitch movement on the straight-tone notes (Ternström and Friberg 1989 model; amplitude from choir singers told to sing straight), moving the fold stiffnesses (three on the two-mass cards, all four on the body-cover fold) and set for each two-mass card.

Fast pitch movement on the straight-tone notes, a second row in the same tension: the 18 to 33 Hz part of the movement Ternström and Friberg 1989 print for singers told to sing straight, 1.34 to 1.76 cents by vowel, read by eye from their Fig. 5, which is solid only to about 25 Hz and has no man at C4 or F4. It was sized once from each two-mass card's gain at 4 Hz and not iterated, so it reads 0.86 to 1.54 cents, the lowest on F4-a's body-cover fold, and no recording enters. The recordings' fast movement looks like pitch at F4, but at C3 and C4 much of it doesn't, so part of what this row closes there may be noise in the recording.

Vibrato on the phrases only, in place of the slow pitch row, with the fast row added under it on the same fold tension (adding the two is our choice; no print sets it): 5.9 Hz and +-69.5 cents, the means of 50 professional singers (Larrouy-Maestri, Magis and Morsomme 2014).

A glottal jet noise row (Verge 1995 flue-jet constant, extrapolated to the glottis). Its gate is a flow threshold, so it sounds for part of each note at C4 and F4, only briefly at C3, and not at all on the C3 /i/ page.

Pulse shimmer on 13 of the 14 graded notes (not C4-u-rigid, which isn't re-rendered) and on the phrases: a per-cycle gain on the glottal pulse, sd 1.13 %, sized from the 1.28 % local shimmer Yoo et al. 2002 report for 65 classical singing students (abstract only; that figure's tracker floor wasn't taken out).
Breath pressure that rises over 150 ms, the centre of a speech range (Fant and Kruckenberg 2005), and is then held.
Folds retrimmed per card on the model alone: only the fold stiffnesses move (three on the two-mass cards, four on F4-a), no recording enters, and the tract's passive formants don't change.
physics_missing: The singer's own tract: these are one man's spoken vowels, and larynx height, pharynx and lip shape differ in singing. The spectrum's tilt follows his vowels, not the singers', and 1-2 kHz is further from the recordings than on the earlier cards on most pages.

The recordings' noise floor: 9 pages are still cleaner than their recordings, by 2.7 to 14.8 dB, and 5 are less clean, by 0.7 to 5.1 dB, F4-o by the most. Read against each band's own lines, the floor between them sits under the recording's on 11 of the 14 notes at 80 Hz to 1 kHz, 11 at 1-2 kHz, 13 at 2-4 kHz and all 14 at 4-8 kHz, and at 8-10 kHz on all 13 whose recording has lines there to read against. The jet noise row and the pulse shimmer are the only sources of energy between the lines on these cards, and we haven't shown what the recordings' floor is. Between the lines at 300 Hz to 2 kHz, on the lossless clips, ours falls with distance from the nearest line by 7.7 dB on average at C3 and 1.1 dB at F4 and stays within 1 dB on average at C4, while the recordings' stay within 1 dB at all three; ours falls at least 3 dB further than the recording's on 5 of the 14 pages. Very roughly a third of the recordings' floor moves with the cycle, what stays isn't shown to be noise, and the printed aspiration level, tried on two pages, moves it by under .1 dB.
Words, consonants and moving tract shapes: tract shape and fold settings are fixed within a render, and each join between vowels in the phrases is a crossfade.
The slow pitch row under vibrato on the phrases: the fast row is added to the vibrato there, but the slow row isn't carried. There are no register changes or formant-tuning gestures.

The singers' tuning and pitch movement: the cards are trimmed to the written note and sit -12.5 to +7.9 cents from equal temperament, while the recordings sit -48.4 to +10.0 cents from it. The period swing over the middle of a clip is 19.5 to 44.2 cents (5-95 %), against 11.5 to 100.6 cents in the recordings.
A sung onset: the pressure rise is a speech value from one male speaker, and no adduction gesture is entered. Attacks read 26 to 93 ms against 22 to 580 ms in the recordings.

Fold tissue: lumped cards, two-mass on the phrases and 13 of the 14 notes and Story and Titze's three-mass body-cover on F4-a, not continuous layered tissue or a 3-D fold. The damping and collision values are printed typical values of one model each, not measurements of a voice, and one stiffness scale per card stands in for a fold-elongation law; the body-cover report moves pitch with Titze and Story's 2002 muscle rules, which aren't open.

Lungs and trachea: the subglottal pressure is an authored player input on each card, not a measured one, with no lung or trachea coupling. Printed airway geometry is in hand (Weibel's symmetric model as printed in Saab et al. 2021, arXiv:2111.07627), but the per-generation wall data (Habib et al. 1994) is not open, and without it the computed airway load does not match the measured one.
Tract acoustics beyond a single series chain of plane-wave sections: no cross-modes, nasal coupling or side branches.
His tense /u/: the engine's frequency check refuses that tract, so lax /u/ stands in.

The wall's detail: it's uniform along the tract, not a measured distribution, and its stiffness is an assumption because the source neglects it. His first formants on these cards sit 49 to 63 Hz above the print's measured ones. That gap is the wall and 37 C air against a rigid model at room temperature, and we haven't split the two.
Head and torso: an infinite baffle replaces them, so there's no head diffraction. The receiver's resolved band is 8 kHz, so energy above that isn't a prediction.
A measured breath: the tract air is a declared physiological state, not a cited measurement.
Convergence on these cards: no ladder has been run on the tract cards, and the fold clock's earlier ladder used a different tract and law.
